Review 3 (rated 2/5): "http://www.hipsterbookclub.com/review... 
 In the memoir Committed: A Skeptic Makes Peace with Marriage, Elizabeth Gilbert approaches the topic of matrimony from a variety of angles: historical, sociological, psychological, and emotional. The idea behind the book holds promise, particularly in a time when marriage is scrutinized and on the cusp of evolution. Unfortunately, Gilbert never makes sense of all the facts and views she collects, and the book leaves the author confused and readers unfulfilled. 
 When the United States Department of Homeland Security denies her Brazilian lover and life partner access into the country, Gilbert must reexamine their relationship. Until that point, the two had maintained a fulfilling but unconventional relationship that satisfied their desire for companionship and independence. As survivors of painful and tedious divorces, the two had mutually rejected the concept of marriage altogether. In Gilbert's words, "We had sworn with all our hearts to never, ever, under any circumstances, marry." Faced with the choice of legal commitment or separation, they reluctantly agree to wed. 
 Playing off the momentum of her well-received 2006 book, Eat, Pray, Love, her latest account follows a similar formula. Anticipating the lengthy legal process before them and unable to be together in the United States, the couple travels through Australia and Southeast Asia. Gilbert capitalizes on this experience by interviewing women she meets in her travels on the topic of marriage, and she combines these first-hand accounts with research into the history of marriage as she attempts to make sense of a concept she wholly rejects. 
 One cannot fault the author for her skepticism. With outrageous divorce rates and the changing landscape of relationships, many question whether marriage is still an essential function of our culture. Historically, men and women took vows out of economic necessity or religious obligation. As Gilbert points out, today we benefit from more social, financial, and spiritual freedoms. Why, then, are we still choosing marriage? 
 Gilbert seeks not only clarity but also reassurance, claiming, "This entire book--every single page of it--has been an effort to search through the complex history of Western marriage until I could find some small place of comfort in there for myself." Fair enough. Where Gilbert struggles, however, is creating a story meaningful enough for an audience. 
 In fact, the author admits she wrote the book for 27 women in her life, including her stepdaughter, mother, and friends. She spends much of the book airing her views on companionship, marriage, and motherhood, much like one would vent frustrations to a close friend. More than once, she admittedly falls into rants. At times, her arguments produce thought-provoking and interesting points for the reader's consideration. A bride-to-be could benefit from contemplating a personal definition of marriage based on Gilbert's research of wedlock throughout history and cultures. However, many of the author's ramblings come off as self-indulgent tirades. 
 For example, Gilbert's diatribe on motherhood comes across as unbalanced and unnecessary. Though not a mother herself, she conveys the strain motherhood places on women. By divulging the personal sacrifices made by her mother and grandmother in the name of family, Gilbert resolves that an independent career woman like herself might better fill the role of "auntie." The entire section, though, feels like an excuse for Gilbert to justify her choice to remain childless and adds little to the overall discussion on matrimonial commitment: 
 I can see where I have been vital sometimes as a member of the Auntie Brigade... there are people I've been able to help, sometimes fully supporting them for years, because I am not obliged, as a mother would be obliged, to put all my energies and resources into the full-time rearing of a child... thereby freeing up resources to spread more widely across the community. In this way, I, too, foster life. 
 The lack of authority and reliability from the author detracts from the more interesting features of the book, such as the conversations with married women from different cultural backgrounds. She only scratches the surfaces with her interviews and then quickly drops the subject, as if she doesn't know how to process the information. Gilbert readily admits that she is not a "professional academic, nor a sociologist, nor a psychologist, nor an expert on marriage." The jumbled facts and figures presented throughout the book are interesting bits of trivia but also incomplete. For all her rants, interviews, and research, Gilbert achieves no clarity. She remains a skeptic until the end and concludes that marriage has changed throughout history and the dynamics of commitment differ between every couple. It required a journey throughout foreign lands and a year's worth of research to reach such an ironically noncommittal conclusion? 
 In Eat, Pray, Love, Gilbert inspired readers by emotionally connecting with them through her personal triumphs and losses. In Committed, her constant bellyaching and condescending attitude distance her from the audience and bury the smattering of noteworthy discourse. By the end of the book, readers will feel more sympathy for her patient husband than the confused and pessimistic Gilbert. Perhaps the book should have stayed between the 27 intended readers because it ultimately offers little wisdom or weight for an audience at large."

My main issue with the book is that at no point do any of the three main characters - Kirby, Dan, and Harper Curtis - ever become more than descriptions on the page. All three exist only insomuch as the author is telling you they do so: they don't become real or three dimensional in the mind of the reader, and neither does their world. The Harper character in particular was annoying because he never achieves any sort of depth: he's a serial killer like pretty much any other serial killer you've ever read about or seen on television. He does bad stuff just because. We know nothing about his background or anything about his life before or after his experience in the House that somehow just pushes him over the line from really bad guy to serial killer. The author offers up one scene that describes some minor animal torture and watching his brother get crushed under a tractor but again, it's par for the course for any serial killer and it offers nothing insightful about *this* particular serial killer. 
 At the start of the book, Harper is running away from a group of people out to do him some sort of harm but it's basically irrelevant in terms of learning anything about him. It's a very drawn out sequence of events, the purpose of which is just to get him to the House where he has this sensory experience while high on morphine that somehow just puts him on this path to hunting and killing the 'shining girls'. And that's about it for Harper in the character development front: he spends the rest of the book stalking and killing girls, and a few other people along the way because that's what serial killers do. At no point does he question what that transformative experience might have been about, or the very idea that this house is somehow a time traveling device/portal. He just immediately goes along with the entire situation. Alrighty, then. 
 Kirby isn't much better. She's a typical alternative/punky kind of girl who doesn't really fit in with mainstream society. Her history with the serial killer doesn't help matters but really, we're not offered much in the way of character development to know her better or sympathize with her much more than that. We get some scenes from her life as she grows up with her flakey, artistic mother Rachel. As an adult she's on the hunt for the man who tried to kill her but the sleuthing/mystery aspect of her story is woefully underdeveloped. Much like the characters in this story, the meat of the plot doesn't get much deeper than the page it's written on. Kirby doesn't really get far at all in terms of finding clues or making connections to Harper until near the end when the whole thing suddenly comes together for apparently no other reason than the author figured it was time to wrap things up. There's a really jarring chapter near the end where Kirby is in the House (which up to this point she didn't even know existed), hiding upstairs as she hears Harper (she doesn't know who he is then but knows he's the man who tried to kill her) coming in and up the stairs. This scene just pops up out of nowhere, and I actually flipped back a few pages to see if I missed something, or if this was supposed to be something she was dreaming about. No, it's just a weird prelude to later on near the end of the book when Kirby actually does find the House and goes inside. It was just a very strange choice structurally as the reader gets thrown right out of things. 
 Another small bit that frustrated me was an exchange near the end between Kirby and the police - she's pointed them to where Harper is living and having been in the House herself, she's seen how it's so different inside than out. Of course, the police go there and it's just a dilapidated abandoned house, inside and out. Review 2 (rated 5/5): "This is an amazing story because even though the inspector figured out, over two other amateur professionals that all the suspects did it -- he also saw the foresight of allowing the train official decide to allow a willing suspect to take all the blame for the murder, as does all the other suspects. 
 This is a story that ties hope, courage, self-sacrifice and bravery with the authority being "wise" enough to cover up a sensational story and thus ruin the least amount of lives... because some criminals are that horrible. This is a world in which man -- not God decides what is correct. That even with technical accuracy and precise reasoning, man still decides to do: what is in his own self interest -- that all choices are a personal matter and not founded/justified on universality. 
 This is how the horrors and the sublime justices are one and the same: that power is bestowed by position and not by some universal good. This is a world where beauty and evil require that we forget one or the other, and in the end this is what is most shocking... Agatha Christie takes us to a deep place that is not easily left. In a sense the mystery unresolved through reasoning so clear, we see everyone's (except the dead's) point of view, so that the evil are the dead only because having all other points of view on the same page establishes what is real. That's how all the weak good guys need each other to defeat the evil bad guy. That's how ideology excludes one of us. That's how only acceptance is good, and the material body of the spirit is the consensus of those who count. 
 For us to be all spirit, we require an invisible reminder to be excluded. The evil marks the border of a transcendental bubble that contains only what can be accepted as being a certain way. This necessary nothing is what is required to establish the minor difference between differences. The question then becomes, what nothing is each nothing -- or are they all the same? Did society truly condemn this man to die, or is the authority afraid of this group? We shall never know. 
 This is a rich book that can be seen in a variety of ways. The solution to this mystery and its subsequent resolution crystalizes the relationships in a way that is undeniably true. In this sense, a mystery is a very detailed account of truth through pure reasoning, but only because the book ends, and then we cannot know everything or anything. We then know the limit of this reasoning, which is what the detective is supposed to find -- exploit and then present the deeper Truth which is reasoning. 
 In that sense, the Godel number as the limit of reasoning is the detective finding another person's will as their undiscountable difference."

A quest for truth that leads to death, madness or disappearance for those who seek to solve it. The Lost City of Z is a blockbuster adventure narrative about what lies beneath the impenetrable jungle canopy of the Amazon. 
 After stumbling upon a hidden trove of diaries, New Yorker writer David Grann set out to solve "the greatest exploration mystery of the 20th century": What happened to the British explorer Percy Fawcett & his quest for the Lost City of Z? 
 I will answer that last question quite simply - no one knows. After some 350 pages, this book answers nothing. But, that wasn't the worst part of the book (although it was extremely annoying)...

Review 5 (rated 5/5): "This book is as close to non-fiction perfection as I have seen in a long time! Though the story is rather simple, Grann's writing makes the events come alive better than any novel I have read in the recent past. Basically, the tale is about the 1920s explorer Percy Fawcett who has discovered new lands across South America in a time far before satellites, GPSs, and even radio. Fawcett is attracted to dangerous adventures especially those that take place in the Amazon. For years, he had studied the Amazon and determined that there was a lost city inside the tropics that he called "Z". Others may be familiar with this city as El Dorado. For decades, Fawcett had explored in a similar area but was never able to find "Z". Finally, in 1925 (as a man in his middle ages), he decides to find the City of Z or die trying. Along with him, he brings his son and his son's best friend. Without spoiling anything in the book, Grann announces this in his first chapter, Fawcett dies on this expedition. Yet, he does not go forgotten! For decades later, even into 2005, people went searching for Fawcett and the city. However, the majority of these explorers also never returned. After researching Fawcett and his personal life, Grann becomes infected with the "Fawcett bug" as he calls it and decides that he too must follow in Fawcett's footsteps and try to discover the city in Fawcett's honor. 
 Though this seems like a nonfiction thriller, it is so much more. Grann is able to place Fawcett in with his contemporaries and show the reader how Fawcett's obsession with the region made him a better explored than even the man on Shakleton's expedition. Though Fawcett is not an entirely likable guy, Grann makes the reader sympathize with his neurosis and find compassion for the man who basically forced his family into poverty in order to feed his adrenaline rush (of course Fawcett was more complex than that). 
 www.iamliteraryaddicted.blogspot.com 
 What sets this piece apart from others about Fawcett is Grann's ability to give the reader in depth knowledge on contemporary times while still making the piece read like a thriller. In addition, Grann was given access to Fawcett's family members which in turn gave him access to some of Fawcett's journals and letters that have never before been shown to people outside of the FAcett family. Grann gives the reader a history of the Royal Geographic Society that is as interesting as it is informative. In addition, he brings the reader into the Amazon with just background and description that his audience feels a connection to the region in a similar way as Fawcett did. Overall, Grann is an excellent writer and this piece really shows his abilities. In addition, Fawcett is a superb subject that keeps explorers and readers coming back for more.  The Monuments Men were a group of art experts assigned the chaotic task of assessing buildings and art pieces for damage in the wake of two armies battling through historic cities. Doing their best with no backup, no special rank, and no transportation, the Monuments Men acted to preserve the great works of art the Germans had been looting in occupied territories. 
 Heartbreaking destruction, of not only human lives but also the history of Europe, followed the clash of Axis and Allies. Hitler and his cronies embarked on an unimaginably complex and widespread scheme to despoil the riches of the occupied territories. The Nazis burned modern art by Picasso, stole from Jewish families, and absconded with anything thought to reflect German heritage. War usually entails looting, but the scale of this plot is breathtaking. 
 The more I learn about Hitler, the more he seems like a maniac straight out of Saturday morning cartoons. He coveted great works of art, was endlessly embittered by the Treaty of Versailles, believed in grand symbolic gestures, planned on enslaving eastern Europe and playing in the rest, tried to exterminate entire classes of people, and named his new government the Thousand-Year Reich. He did everything short of strapping on a cape and cackling "I have you now!" to Superman. 
 The list of art the Nazis stole included Michelangelo's "Bruges Madonna", the massive and massively important Ghent Altarpiece, Vermeer's "The Astronomer", Rembrandt's enormous oil painting "The Night Watch", and the Bayeux Tapestry - plus thousands of other works of art, pieces of jewelry, statues, porcelain, furniture, and gold. These valuables were hidden in salt mines and other unlikely places throughout Germany, including the famous mine in Altaussee. 
 Against this seemingly unstoppable machine of destruction and theft stood the few lone Monuments Men, determined to restore order and put the art world to right again. It was a race against time, especially given the fact that many of his stooges interpreted Hitler's infamous Nero Decree to extend to the stolen art he had amassed for his dream of a Fuhrermuseum in Linz, Austria. 
 Interspersed with tales of Monuments Men exploits are letters they sent to loved ones and colleagues (all a cut above the average soldier's letter), charting the excitement and then the increasing jadedness of the Monuments Men as they struggled to do their jobs single-handedly on the frontlines of a horrific war. 
 Edsel also tells the tale of the remarkable Frenchwoman Rose Valland, whose ferocious determination and subtle spycraft ensured that the patrimony of France did not simply disappear into the night. She is the only female member of the Monuments Men (and not an official one), and without her tireless efforts the impact of the war would have been even more devastating to the art community than it proved to be. 
 In fact, the aftermath of World War II is still with us, in lost lives and destroyed artworks. As proof, I offer two recent articles about hoards discovered more than 70 years later. This story is so vast it almost seems unbelievable. The book begins slowly, but soon picks up, with the author's passion for his subject showing through on every page. (He points out, rightly, that we could have used a Monuments unit in Baghdad after the 2003 invasion.) Essential reading for anyone interested in art and war.

While he had the conqueror's mentality - he believed he was entitled to the spoils of war, and he was determined to have them - Hitler and the Nazis had gone to great lengths to establish new laws and procedures to 'legalize' the looting activities that would follow. This included forcing the conquered countries to give him certain works as a term of their surrender." - 150

 "Just seeing the warehouses the Nazis had filled with 'confiscated' items brought home to him the size and complexity of their looting operation. This wasn't accidental damage or angry retaliation, but an enormous web of deliberate deceit that stretched all over Paris and down all the roads back to the Fatherland and all the way to Hitler's office in Berlin." - 239 
 "To save the culture of your allies is a small thing. To cherish the culture of your enemy, to risk your life and the life of other men to save it, to give it all back to them as soon as the battle was won...it was unheard of, but that is exactly what Walker Hancock and the other Monuments Men intended to do." - 321

 When I studied English Literature in college, I would frequently be reading five works of literature at one time. Occasionally, I would have a night where I ignored all of my school work/reading and would blaze through a YA novel in one night. I'm not sure if it's because I'm not reading classic literature as much or because this one just wasn't that good, but Glass Sword just didn't do it for me. 
 The whole book felt uninspired. It is a lesser version of The Hunger Games. Instead of having a clear vision like Katniss (who just wants her family to be safe), Mare bounces around between her own self-interest, guilt, and a supposed goal of trying to save the newbloods (who are dropped in as a plot point that isn't even fully realized). 
 This book is truly a testament to aggressive YA PR campaigns. It lacks even the most basic elements that make a good YA palate cleanser. Instead of having a clear romance plot (a love triangle would even be acceptable!), Glass Sword has a messy square with no payoff. Mare loves Cal, but Cal doesn't love her (something that is an obvious lie). Kiliorn loves Mare, but she doesn't love him (which feels thrown in for shock value). Finally, Mare still loves Maven, the boy who betrayed her and continues to kill her people. This part of the wonky love square could have been interesting if it had any real consequences. Instead, it just softens the blow of the fake cliff-hanger ending. 
 The whole book, Mare is an uninteresting and selfish narrator. She is constantly focused on her pain, which could have been at least mildly compelling. But instead of showing us the consequences of the trauma that Mare experienced, Aveyard instead tells us everything. She must have no trust in her readers at all. Either that, or she completely lacks the ability to write well. I know I've never written and published a novel and I might not have room to talk. But I learned that the first rule of writing was to show, not tell. 
 Another way Aveyard's lack of decent writing shines through is in her treatment of the newbloods.  The upper class apparently have balls and wear corsets and big ball gowns and tails and top hats. They have rooms that are replicas of early 1900 architecture and even lighting. The Icarus was essentially the Titanic in space. But they have tons of money and electricity and hover trays and all kinds of technology. So why is there wardrobe and way of interacting with each other reversed back to over a hundred years ago? No one knows. Meanwhile the peasants wear like jeans and stuff but they have no electricity and live very primitively. Except like Tarver's mom and dad who were a poet and a college professor by trade. If they were as rural and "backwoods" as Tarver portrayed them wouldn't they have been small farmers or laborers? Anyway, basically nothing added up. I couldn't ever figure out why the lower class would have no electricity. They didn't seem to be all that poor and certainly weren't downtrodden or starving. I also couldn't figure out if the upper and lower classes even shared the same planets. 
 On the planet that Tarver and Lilac crash on, there is ONE mountain lion and that's it? If the planet was abandoned and mountain lions are the only predator wouldn't it be overrun? Or wouldn't they have all died off because there is no mention of any other kind of animal except "small burrowing things" that didn't sound like they'd be enough to sustain mountain lions long term? Okay, two examples is enough. But there were a lot more. 
 After the big crash, which happens fairly quickly, the book is just Tarver and Lilac wandering alone on this abandoned planet. Nothing else really happens to them. It's not even an interesting, unique planet. They could have been wandering through any random forest down here on regular old earth, except they probably would have run across more predators. Up until about half way through I was interested and even intrigued. Then things started to get a little weird and ridiculous. It bugged me SO much that Tarver held on to her so hard knowing that she was really just an imitation. I'm not even going to go into how little sense all that made.  **MILD SPOILERS HEAD** 
 The things I liked 
 Nikolai has his strengths as the enchanter and Vika has her own strengths Nikolai can control Material things and Vika the Natural Elements . They each have 5 rounds and at the end of the game the one who loses dies i.e if they don't kill each other before that...  I really liked Pasha's sister as she is really clear in what she wants. I think she is actually fit to be a Queen when she grows up.

The reader will not find any dramatic twists and turns. 
 However, Dracula has not aged as well as some of the other classics. Stoker's prose has an archaic feel to it that works very well at times but can come off as plodding and overly wrought at others. The popularity of Dracula also means that the story itself is largely spoiled - the reader is almost certainly going to know what happens due to exposure to the many (and highly variable in quality) adaptations of the novel. 
 Dracula is a must read for any fan of classical horror. Its importance to the field alone would necessitate at least one reading by the horror aficionado.  And that's despite the fact that it's a middle-grade* novel that would only take a couple hours of dedicated reading to get through. 
 The characters are all flat and predictable -- naively enthused protagonist, endearingly-cluttered professor mentor, irritable and artsy female foil, snidely aloof professor red herring, militant investigator... Not a one is all that memorable. The mystery element might be intriguing, if readers had any reason at all to care about the Rithmatists-in-training who have been killed, or about any of those at risk of being targeted next, but none of them is shown in any detail. Our protagonist, in fact, is notable mainly because he doesn't fit the killer's profile -- not very conducive to raising the tension. 
 The one highlight of the book is, as in so many of Sanderson's books, the worldbuilding. Both the altered history and the magic system have heaps of intriguing potential -- but not nearly enough to get me to keep reading when none of the other elements inspire anything but yawns. 
 So I'm throwing in the towel. One star, and I'm clearing it from my currently-reading shelf. Better luck next time. 
 *I consider this book middle-grade, despite its marketing as YA, because there's really nothing even remotely teenagerly about it -- no hormones, no feel of being on the brink of adulthood.  -Even though she blamed Cole for what happened, she also took responsibility for her actions in it.

Review 3 (rated 5/5): "This book is stunningly beautiful.From the writing and characters to the flawless blending of myth and reality, it is perfect. Not to mention the gorgeous cover, I mean, really, what girl doesn't dream of a dress like that? 
 What caught me most was the writing. It was dramatic and completely character-centric. No unnecessary words or long, rambling paragraphs. Yet it never felt rushed and flowed naturally throughout. I loved how the author managed to portray such intense emotions with such subtlety. I also truly love what she did with two of my favorite myths, Orpheus and Eurydics and Hades and Persephone. 
 Nikki is wonderful. She's so quiet that you don't always notice, but she has a will of steel. Knowing that she has little time before she is lost to torment and death, her greatest wish is to make it easier on the people she leaves behind. Especially for Jack. 
 Ah, Jack. My favorite character. He's a really, really nice guy with hints of a rebel that sneak out with an eyebrow piercing. He doesn't know where Nikki has been for so long, but he knows that she's been hurt. So he is what she needs most; a friend. He never pushes too hard, but he never gives up. He may take a step back at certain revelations, but never for more than a moment. 
 Cole is an entirely different kettle of fish. He's dark through and through, and has undoubtedly done terrible things, but is he completely irredeemable? Perhaps, perhaps not. It should be...interesting. 
 I would recommend this book to just about anyone, but especially lovers of mythology and beautiful, beautiful romance. And to people who don't mind shedding a few tears over a magnificent ending.

Review 8 (rated 1/5): "This is a book that had the potential to be wonderfully amazing. I'm not one to obsess over covers because I really honestly don't care, but the cover for this was gorgeous. The main factor in my picking this up though was the premise. I read the back of the book and I was digging the whole Everneath concept. I'm a sucker for mythology and I was interested to see what kind of spin the author would take on the Persephone tale. Sadly, I have to say that I was super disappointed. It had all the components to be a fun book, but I felt a little let down. The characters were bland and I didn't connect to any of them. It also seemed liked nothing much happened, which was surprising for a book where the main character is on a time limit to save her soul. It was pretty much Nikki hanging out knitting and awkwardly staring at her ex, Jack. It wasn't until a great deal in the book where things started happening and even then, it was a lot of back and forth. Of course, the whole time Nikki was determined to damn her soul to the Tunnels of the Everneath. I was like, 'Is she serious?!'. Sure, Cole's kind of freaky, but the guy is nowhere bad enough for her to be so resistant to his offer. I'm sorry but if I had the choice between eternal life and being buried alive in hell, I'd for sure be running off with Cole. Just saying. Her doing what she was doing was just stubborn and stupid. The longer I read, I just wanted her to throw herself into the Tunnels already and end the book. The ending itself was a little lackluster. I have a feeling I was supposed to be heartbroken by how things played out, but I wasn't. 
 The main character Nikki was boring personified. Gahh, I swear that she had no personality whatsoever. I could get through a slightly underwhelming book plot if the characters are realistic and have some life to them. Nikki was the type of protagonist I hate reading about. She came off as a lethargic blob of a person who wandered about wasting time. Not that every protagonist has to be a kickass pillar of strength, but at least make them have some kind of spark. I have no clue what Nikki even looks like, which shouldn't be such a big deal, but I also have no insight whatsoever into her as a person. Looking back, I honestly have no clue what things she likes or dislikes, what she wants to do in her life, etc. Aside from the car accident thing, I virtually knew nothing about her. She was just some cardboard person bumbling about the storyline. 
 As for the two guys Jack and Cole, I didn't feel either of them. They didn't have much of a personality either. I'll admit I kind of liked the two of them in the flashbacks Nikki had, but any life the characters had were thrown out in the present part of the book. Nikki had these two guys fighting over her and I couldn't understand it. Cole I could kind of love because he had ulterior motives for the things he was saying and doing. He's not a nice guy really. I mean, the guy feeds off people's souls. However, the author had to ruin things by making Cole some obsessive, love-struck boy. I would much rather Cole didn't like Nikki and was just using her for his whole power ploy. Jack also was a bit cardboard. He was just there. I didn't feel the connection between him and Nikki either. All the words were being said, but it didn't feel real to me. The two of them were made to seem 'so in love', whirlwind romance or whatever and it wasn't to me. Jack and Jules should have hooked up because they seemed better together than him and Nikki. 
 Overall, I didn't really like this at all. I don't want to bash because it wasn't even close to being the worst thing I've ever read. That goes to 'Personal Demons' by Lisa Desrochers. However, it was sort of disappointing. The premise itself sounded interesting, but the execution was kind of terrible. I hate to be mean, but I feel like this would have been a lot better if someone other than the author would have written it. The concept was there, but the characters needed to developed more and just in general I wanted more depth. I want to read a book that makes me fall in love with all the characters, both good and bad. I want to care about what's happening and this book was lacking all that for me. It seems like a ton of people are in love with this book and good for them, but it just wasn't for me and I'm defintely not going to read the next one."
